title: Does Permanent Lighting Increase Home Value? An Honest Look for Ontario Homeowners
metaTitle: Does Permanent Lighting Add Home Value? | Forever Lights
metaDescription: Does permanent LED roofline lighting increase home value? An honest look at curb appeal, dusk listing photos, buyer perception and resale in London, Ontario.
excerpt: Permanent roofline lighting is often sold as a home-value upgrade. Here is a straight answer on curb appeal, dusk listing photos, buyer perception, energy cost, durability, what realtors actually say, and how to hand the system over to a buyer.

keyTakeaways: Permanent lighting is not a renovation that shows up as a line item on an appraisal. Its value is in how the home presents, particularly at dusk and in listing photos, and in what buyers assume about a house that looks cared for.
Twilight photography is one of the most effective tools in a listing, and a home with clean roofline lighting is ready for it on any evening without a stylist.
Buyers see a permanent, warrantied, app-controlled system as a finished feature they will never have to install, which is a different conversation from a box of light strings in the garage.
Low running cost, IP68 sealed fixtures rated to minus 40 degrees, 50,000-hour LEDs and a transferable warranty make it a feature that survives the inspection and the first winter.
Compared with other exterior upgrades, permanent lighting is a smaller, faster job that changes the look of the whole house rather than one part of it.

body.text: Ask whether permanent LED lighting increases home value and you will get two unhelpful answers. One promises a specific percentage on your sale price, which nobody can honestly do; the other says buyers do not pay for decoration, which misses how homes actually sell. The truth sits in between. This guide takes the question seriously for homeowners in London and across Southwestern Ontario: what permanent lighting does for curb appeal and listing photos, how buyers and realtors tend to see it, what it costs to own, and how it compares with the other things you could spend the money on before a sale.
Two kinds of value, and which one this is

It helps to separate appraised value from market appeal. Appraised value is what a lender's appraiser assigns from comparable sales, square footage, lot, bedrooms and condition. Exterior lighting rarely moves that number in a measurable way, and you should be wary of anyone who says otherwise. Market appeal is different: how many people come to the showing, how they feel walking up the driveway, how the listing photo performs against the twenty others a buyer scrolled past that night, and whether the home gets an offer in the first week or sits. That is where permanent lighting does its work.
Curb appeal after dark

Most curb appeal advice is about daytime, but in Ontario a large share of showings, drive-bys and first visits happen after work, and from November through March that means after dark. A house with only a porch light disappears into the street at 6:00 PM. A house with a warm white line of light tracing the roofline, gables and entrance reads as finished, intentional and looked-after. It highlights the architecture the owner paid for and hides nothing. Buyers who see a home at its best at night are more likely to book a daytime showing, and more likely to arrive already inclined to like it. Curb appeal is not about being the brightest house on the street; it is about being the house that looks like someone cared.
Listing photos at dusk

Real estate photographers have long known that the twilight shot, taken in the few minutes after sunset when the sky is still deep blue and the house is lit from within and without, is the photo that stops a scroll. It is also the hardest to get. It needs the photographer back at a specific time, every interior light on, and ideally exterior lighting that flatters the house.

A home with permanent roofline lighting is ready for a real twilight photo on any evening of the year. The owner sets warm white at a moderate brightness, the photographer arrives at dusk, and the house looks the way it looks every night. That photo becomes the hero image on the listing, the social post and the feature sheet, without a stylist or a retoucher. For a winter listing in London, when most homes photograph flat and grey after 5:00 PM, it can be the difference between a listing that gets noticed and one that does not.
What buyers actually see

Walk a buyer through what they encounter and the value case gets clearer. At the showing, they see a clean line of colour-matched aluminum track under the soffit that in daylight reads as trim. They are told it is a permanent system with individually addressable RGBW LEDs, controlled from a phone app with scenes and schedules, that it runs Christmas, Halloween, Canada Day and everyday warm white, and that it carries a warranty. What they hear is that a project they might have thought about doing is already done, professionally, and that they will never spend a November on a ladder.

items: It signals maintenance. A home with a well-installed permanent system tends to be read as a home where other things were done properly too.
It removes a future task. Buyers with young families in particular respond to features that save time and eliminate ladders.
It is a talking point. Agents like features they can demonstrate, and switching a roofline from warm white to red and green from a phone during a showing is memorable.
It is not polarising when done tastefully. A colour-matched track and a warm white default do not read as a style choice a buyer has to undo.

body.text: Security and safety lighting as a selling feature

There is a practical side that resonates with buyers who are not thinking about holidays at all. A roofline system on a dusk-to-dawn or dusk-to-bedtime schedule lights the entire perimeter of the house, not just the front door: lit steps, lit walkways, lit driveways and no dark corners at the side of the garage. It also means the house looks occupied when the owners are away, because the schedule runs whether anyone is home or not. For many buyers this is the feature that lands first, and it costs nothing extra because it is the same system.
Energy cost: a feature, not a liability

A cautious buyer will ask what the lights cost to run, and the honest answer works in your favour. Each LED point draws about 0.3 watts, so even a full roofline running warm white for an evening uses far less than the incandescent holiday displays of a generation ago, and the app's dimming and scheduling keep real-world use well below the maximum. It is closer to leaving a few household bulbs on than to running an appliance.
Durability: why it survives the inspection
Buyers and home inspectors are rightly suspicious of things bolted to a house that might fail or leak. A quality permanent system answers those concerns directly:

items: The track is extruded aluminum, which does not rust, acts as a heat sink for the LEDs and is fastened to the soffit or fascia rather than through the roof.
Fixtures are sealed to IP68 and rated to operate down to minus 40 degrees Celsius, which covers anything a Southwestern Ontario winter produces.
Components are CSA-approved and the system connects to an existing GFCI-protected outlet, so no permit is required and there is no change to the home's electrical panel.
The LEDs are rated for 50,000 hours, which at a few hours a night is decades of use.
Our installs carry a 5-year parts warranty and a 1-year workmanship warranty, and a buyer inherits a system that a local company is still standing behind.

body.text: What realtors actually say

We work with agents across the London area and hear a consistent picture, with the caveat that it is opinion from practice rather than a study. Agents generally do not claim exterior lighting adds a specific dollar figure to a sale, and you should be sceptical of any that do. What they do say is that exterior lighting is one of the lower-cost ways to lift how a home presents, that dusk photography sells, that buyers respond to homes that look cared for, and that anything which makes a listing distinctive in a crowded search helps. Several have told us they list a permanent lighting system on the feature sheet the same way they would a new furnace, because it is a completed, warrantied improvement rather than a promise.
How it compares with other exterior upgrades
Homeowners preparing to sell usually have a short list of exterior projects and a limited budget. Here is how permanent lighting compares with the usual candidates:

items: Front door and garage door replacement: strong daytime curb appeal, a day or two of work, one focal point changed. Permanent lighting changes the whole silhouette and works at night, when many first impressions are formed.
Landscaping and hardscaping: excellent daytime impact, can be slow and costly, and shows best in summer. Roofline lighting looks the same in February as in July, which matters for winter listings.
Exterior painting or new siding: transformative but expensive and disruptive. Lighting is a one-day install with no change to the structure.
Roof replacement: a necessity buyers expect, not a feature they get excited about. Lighting is optional and memorable.
Seasonal Christmas light installation: a recurring cost that leaves nothing behind when you sell. Permanent lighting stays with the house and is part of the sale.
Low-voltage landscape spotlights: a good complement, but they light the ground rather than the architecture and do not change colour for occasions.

body.text: The fair conclusion is that permanent lighting is not a substitute for fixing real problems. A tired roof or peeling paint should come first. But among the optional upgrades that change how a house feels, it is one of the few that is fast, non-structural, works year-round and after dark, and comes with financing over 24 months at 10 percent APR on approved credit. Use our cost estimator for a ballpark on your own roofline, since track length and layout drive the number.
Selling the home: transferring the app and the warranty

What happens to the system at closing is straightforward. The track, controller, transformer and wiring are fixtures attached to the house, so they stay with it like any other built-in. The app account is the only thing that changes hands, and it takes a few minutes:

items: Before closing, save your favourite scenes and schedules, then remove your own account from the controller, or leave the everyday warm-white schedule running so the house is lit for the new owners' first night.
The buyer installs the app and pairs their own account with the controller. If anything is unclear, they can call us at (519) 914-3404 and we will reset the controller and walk them through it.
Leave a note in the buyer's package with the installer's name, install date and warranty terms; our 5-year parts warranty follows the system, so the buyer keeps the remaining coverage.
If the new owners want the colour temperature, brightness or zones changed, it is all done from the app with nothing touched on the house.

body.text: Handled this way, the lighting is a feature the buyer inherits fully working on day one, with a local company behind it, which is the kind of detail that makes a house feel like a good decision after the papers are signed.

So, does permanent lighting increase home value? Not in the way a bathroom or a finished basement shows up on an appraisal, and we will not tell you it does. What it reliably does is make a home in London, St. Thomas, Strathroy, Woodstock, Ingersoll, Tillsonburg or anywhere in Southwestern Ontario present better at the times buyers are looking, photograph better for the listing, signal that the house has been cared for, and hand the buyer a finished, durable, warrantied feature they will use every night. Either way, start with a free site visit at /contact, and the lights will be on before the sign goes up.

faq.q: Does permanent roofline lighting add to a home's appraised value?
faq.a: Not measurably, and you should be cautious of anyone who promises a specific percentage. Its value is in market appeal: how the home presents at dusk, how the listing photos perform, and how buyers perceive a home that looks cared for. Those things affect showings and offers rather than the appraiser's number.

faq.q: Does the lighting stay with the house when I sell?
faq.a: Yes. The aluminum track, controller, transformer and wiring are fixtures attached to the home and transfer with it. The buyer pairs their own phone to the controller through the app, and our 5-year parts warranty follows the system, so they inherit the remaining coverage.

faq.q: Will buyers see permanent lighting as a positive or something they have to remove?
faq.a: When it is installed with colour-matched track and a warm white everyday setting, buyers generally see it as a finished feature rather than a style choice to undo. It reads as trim in daylight and as architectural lighting at night, and it removes a ladder job they would otherwise face every December.

faq.q: Is permanent lighting a better pre-sale investment than landscaping or a new front door?
faq.a: It depends on the home. Fix real problems first. Among optional upgrades, permanent lighting is a one-day, non-structural install that changes the look of the whole house after dark and works the same in winter as in summer, which makes it especially useful for a winter listing. Landscaping and doors are strong daytime improvements that complement it.

faq.q: Does the lighting need a permit or any electrical work that a buyer would ask about?
faq.a: No permit is required when the system connects to your home's existing GFCI-protected outdoor receptacle, which is how we install it. The components are CSA-approved, the fixtures are IP68 sealed and rated to minus 40 degrees, and nothing changes at the electrical panel, so there is nothing unusual for an inspection.
